subject: physics
title: The photoelectric effect
key_idea: When light of high enough frequency hits a metal, it releases electrons. Each photon gives all its energy to one electron. The effect only makes sense if light comes in photons.

sections.heading: What happens at the metal surface

blocks.text: In the photoelectric effect, electromagnetic radiation shining on a metal surface releases electrons from it. The electrons released are called photoelectrons.

items.meaning: The emission of electrons from a metal surface when electromagnetic radiation of high enough frequency is incident on it.
An electron released from a metal surface by the absorption of a photon.

items: Each photon is absorbed by just one electron, in a one-to-one interaction.
The electron takes all of the photon's energy.
Electrons near the surface escape most easily.

blocks.text: A simple demonstration uses a zinc plate on a gold-leaf electroscope.

items: Charge the plate negatively. The gold leaf rises because it is repelled by the plate.
Shine ultraviolet radiation on the zinc. The leaf falls as electrons are emitted and the charge leaks away.
Visible light does not make the leaf fall, however bright it is.
A photon is absorbed by a single electron, which can then leave the metal.
The emitted electrons are called photoelectrons.

blocks.text: An electron needs a minimum energy to escape the surface. If the photon energy is below this, no electron is emitted.

items.meaning: The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of a metal.
The minimum frequency of radiation that causes photoelectric emission from a metal.

items: If f < f₀, no photoelectrons are emitted. This is true however intense the radiation is.
If f > f₀, photoelectrons are emitted at once.
Different metals have different work functions, so different threshold frequencies.
Photoelectric emission needs hf ≥ φ.
Below the threshold frequency there is no emission at any intensity.

blocks.text: Energy is conserved. The photon energy pays for the escape, and any energy left over becomes kinetic energy.

blocks.label: Photoelectric equation
where: Eₖ(max) = maximum kinetic energy of a photoelectron (J)

blocks.text: The maximum kinetic energy can also be written ½mvₘₐₓ², where m is the electron mass and vₘₐₓ its greatest speed.

items: The kinetic energy is a maximum because electrons deeper in the metal lose some energy before they escape.
Eₖ(max) rises linearly with f. It is zero at the threshold frequency.
A graph of Eₖ(max) against f has gradient h and an x-intercept at f₀.

diagram.alt: A slider for the photoelectric effect. Choose a metal and a frequency, then read the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.

items: hf = φ + Eₖ(max).
Eₖ(max) depends on the frequency and the metal, not the intensity.

blocks.text: Intensity is the energy delivered per second per unit area. At a fixed frequency, more intensity means more photons each second.

items: Each photon is absorbed by one electron, so doubling the photons per second doubles the electrons released per second.
The photoelectric current is therefore proportional to intensity, for frequency above the threshold.
Each photon still has the same energy, so Eₖ(max) does not change with intensity.

blocks.text: The photoelectric effect is evidence for the particle nature of radiation. The wave model cannot explain it.

rows: Any frequency works if the wave is intense enough
A photon below f₀ has too little energy for any one electron
Electrons should take time to build up energy
One photon gives one electron all its energy at once
Brighter wave should give more energy
Brighter beam means more photons, not more energy per photon

items: Photoelectric current is proportional to intensity above f₀.
Eₖ(max) is independent of intensity.
The effect is evidence for photons.

checks.q: Explain why no electrons are emitted from a metal when the radiation is below the threshold frequency, however intense it is.
checks.a: Each photon is absorbed by one electron. Below the threshold frequency a photon's energy hf is less than the work function, so no electron can escape. More intensity means more photons, but each still has too little energy.

checks.q: Light of frequency 8.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz hits a metal of work function 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
The intensity of the radiation is doubled at a fixed frequency above f₀. State the effect on the photoelectric current and on Eₖ(max).
checks.a: The photoelectric current doubles. Eₖ(max) is unchanged.

blocks.text: The kinetic energy of the fastest photoelectrons can be linked to a stopping potential.

items.meaning: The potential difference that just stops the fastest photoelectrons reaching the collector.

items: Raising the retarding potential until the current stops gives Vₛ.
The experimental method for finding the stopping potential is not required.
Stopping potential measures Eₖ(max): Eₖ(max) = eVₛ.
A larger stopping potential means faster photoelectrons.

blocks.text: The threshold can also be stated as a wavelength. It is the longest wavelength that causes emission.

items.meaning: The maximum wavelength of radiation that causes photoelectric emission.

items: Wavelength longer than λ₀ means no emission.
Wavelength shorter than λ₀ means emission.
Emission needs f ≥ f₀, or equivalently λ ≤ λ₀.
A long wavelength means low photon energy.
